front_blocks.md: Why is nitrogen gas very unreactive?

back_blocks.md: Nitrogen forms a **triple covalent bond** (N≡N) with a bond enthalpy of 1000 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. This very strong bond requires a large amount of energy to break. Nitrogen is also **nonpolar**, making it unlikely to react with other molecules.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Nitrogen gas is polar because it contains a triple bond.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Nitrogen gas (N≡N) is **nonpolar**. The two identical nitrogen atoms have the same electronegativity, so the electrons are shared equally and there is no overall dipole.

front_blocks.md: Define **Brønsted-Lowry base**.

back_blocks.md: A **Brønsted-Lowry base** is a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) acceptor. **Ammonia** acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base, using its lone pair on nitrogen to accept a proton and form the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>).

cards.back_md: A **Brønsted-Lowry base** is a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) acceptor. **Ammonia** acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base, using its lone pair on nitrogen to accept a proton and form the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>).

front_blocks.md: Describe the shape of ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) and the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>), and explain the difference.

back_blocks.md: **NH**<sub>**3**</sub> has a **pyramidal** shape due to the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen repelling the three bonding pairs. **NH**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+**</sup> has a **tetrahedral** shape because the lone pair has been donated to form a dative bond with H<sup>+</sup>, leaving four equal bonds.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ammonia is a strong base because it reacts completely with water.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Ammonia is a **weak base**. The equilibrium NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) lies well to the **left**, so only a small proportion of NH<sub>3</sub> molecules ionise.

front_blocks.md: How is the presence of ammonium ions in an unknown solution confirmed?

back_blocks.md: The unknown solution is warmed with **calcium hydroxide**. If ammonium ions are present, **ammonia gas** is released. The gas turns **damp red litmus paper blue**, confirming the presence of NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ions.

front_blocks.md: How are nitrogen oxides formed in car engines?

back_blocks.md: Inside a car engine, the high **temperature** and **pressure** cause atmospheric **nitrogen** and **oxygen** to react, forming nitrogen oxides (NO and NO<sub>2</sub>). These are released into the atmosphere through exhaust fumes.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Catalytic converters convert nitrogen oxides into harmless nitrogen gas.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

In a catalytic converter, NO is reduced on the surface of a hot metal catalyst (e.g. platinum): 2CO (g) + 2NO (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + N<sub>2</sub> (g). **N**<sub>**2**</sub> is released as a harmless gas.

front_blocks.md: Define **secondary pollutant**.

back_blocks.md: A **secondary pollutant** is one that is not emitted directly from a source but is formed in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving **primary pollutants**. Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) is an example, formed from nitrogen oxides and VOCs in sunlight.

front_blocks.md: Write the equation showing how NO<sub>2</sub> and water contribute to the formation of acid rain.

back_blocks.md: 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq)
The **nitric acid** dissolves in cloud water droplets. When these fall as rain, the result is **acid rain**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
NO<sub>2</sub> acts as a catalyst in the conversion of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

**NO**<sub>**2**</sub> catalyses the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub>: NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) → SO<sub>3</sub> (g) + NO (g). The NO is then re-oxidised to NO<sub>2</sub>, regenerating the catalyst. SO<sub>3</sub> reacts with water to form H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, contributing to **acid rain**.

front_blocks.md: Distinguish between primary and secondary pollutants, giving one example of each.

back_blocks.md: A **primary pollutant** is emitted directly from a source (e.g. **NO** from car exhausts). A **secondary pollutant** forms through atmospheric reactions between primary pollutants (e.g. **PAN**, formed from VOCs and nitrogen oxides in sunlight).

front_blocks.md: Write the equation for the reaction of NO with oxygen in the atmosphere and explain its environmental significance.

back_blocks.md: 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)

**NO**<sub>**2**</sub> is a more reactive pollutant than NO. It contributes to **acid rain** by reacting with water and oxygen to form HNO<sub>3</sub>, and to **photochemical smog** by reacting with VOCs in sunlight.
